planting.note: Broadcast or drill into warm, medium-to-high fertility soil in full sun well after last frost; Marandu needs consistently warm soil and establishes best during peak summer heat.

directions: Broadcast or drill seed into warm, well-drained soil of medium to high fertility in full sun; Marandu is intolerant of waterlogged ground, unlike some of its Brachiaria relatives. Released by Brazil's Embrapa in 1984 from Zimbabwean germplasm, it became the most widely planted forage cultivar in Brazil thanks to its vigorous tufted growth, deep root system, and rapid regrowth after grazing. Expect pastures to reach first grazing readiness 60-90 days after a warm-season planting, with excellent persistence on degraded tropical soils. It is frost-sensitive and dies back or behaves as an annual outside consistently frost-free zones.

scientific_name: Brachiaria ruziziensis x brizantha x decumbens 'Mulato II'

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into warm, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Mulato II tolerates some seasonal waterlogging better than most Brachiaria cultivars but still needs warm soil to establish.

directions: Sow into warm, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun at 6-10 kg/ha pure live seed; this three-way interspecific hybrid (CIAT accession 36087) was released by CIAT in 2005 and combines a semi-decumbent, stoloniferous habit with notable resistance to spittlebug, a major pest of Brachiaria pastures. Yields run 10-27 tons of dry matter per hectare per year, with first grazing or cutting possible 75-90 days after planting. It works well for pasture renovation, cut-and-carry forage systems, and tropical ground cover on acid soils with marginal fertility.
sources: CIAT / Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto fertile, well-drained soil and lightly cover; Mombaça needs rich soil and consistent warmth to reach its full tall, leafy potential.

directions: Broadcast seed at 5-8 kg/ha pure live seed onto fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and cover lightly; Mombaça was introduced to Brazil from Korogwe, Tanzania in 1993 and is the highest-yielding guinea grass cultivar in common use, producing 20-28 tons of dry matter per hectare per year under good management. This tall, leafy, tufted perennial needs a rotational rest of roughly 40-45 days in the wet season to regrow fully before the next grazing or cutting. It has no frost tolerance and should be treated as a warm-season-only planting outside the tropics and subtropics.

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and cover lightly; like its sibling cultivar Mombaça, Tanzânia-1 shares the same Tanzanian origin and needs rich, warm soil to establish.

directions: Broadcast seed at 5-8 kg/ha pure live seed onto fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; released by Embrapa Beef Cattle in 1990 from the same Korogwe, Tanzania collection as Mombaça, Tanzânia-1 is shorter and leafier with a higher leaf-to-stem ratio, yielding 20-26 tons of dry matter per hectare per year. Use it as a rotational companion to Mombaça to diversify guinea-grass pasture or cover-crop systems and spread grazing pressure across cultivars with slightly different regrowth habits. No frost tolerance; dies back hard with the first freeze.

planting.note: Drill in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil; Perun establishes quickly like a ryegrass but holds on through summer heat and drought with fescue-like deep roots.

directions: Drill 25-35 lb/ac in a pure stand (or 3-20 lb/ac as part of a mix) into fertile, well-drained soil; Perun is a tetraploid hybrid of Italian ryegrass and meadow fescue bred by the Czech institute OSEVA, combining ryegrass's fast 7-10 day establishment and forage quality with fescue's deep rooting and summer drought tolerance. It is a heavy nitrogen feeder, so plan for over 120 lb N/ac across the season to sustain its productivity. Growers commonly use it as a nurse crop for establishing alfalfa or to quickly fill in winter-damaged cool-season pasture and hay stands.

planting.note: Direct sow in rows or broadcast into warm soil after last frost; Chapingo teosinte is a corn relative that needs a full frost-free summer but can be cut for forage or cover well before it would reach seed.

directions: Sow 8-10 lb/ac in rows or 10-12 lb/ac broadcast and lightly disked into warm soil after the last frost; Chapingo is an NRCS Plant Materials Program release of this wild corn relative, valued as a warm-season annual forage and cover crop that produces more biomass than maize under heat or drought stress. Unlike maize it regrows readily after cutting or grazing, supporting multiple harvests in a single season. It needs 165-170 frost-free days to set seed but delivers heavy biomass well before that point, and the first fall frost kills it outright.

planting.note: Establish from seed or sprigs into sandy, low-fertility soil in full sun during warm weather; Survenola is often propagated vegetatively on the Gulf Coast rather than seeded.

directions: Seed or sprig into sandy, low-fertility soil in full sun during warm weather; Survenola was released in Florida in 1982 (PI 421785) as a wide-leaved selection of digitgrass bred for subtropical sand-ridge and Gulf Coast conditions. Once established it tolerates drought well and needs little fertility to persist, making it useful for erosion control and low-input grazing on poor soils. Top growth is killed by hard freezes, but established crowns can survive mild Gulf Coast winters and resume growth in spring.

planting.note: Drill in early spring or late summer into well-drained pasture soil; Tekapo's low, dense crown tolerates close, continuous grazing better than standard orchardgrass.

directions: Drill 10-15 lb/ac in a pure stand or 3-6 lb/ac in grass-legume mixes into well-drained soil; this New Zealand-bred orchardgrass cultivar forms a distinctively low, prostrate crown that holds up to hard, continuous grazing better than taller orchardgrass types. It shows good tolerance of heat, moderate drought, low fertility, and rust, and is fully winter-hardy once established. Use it in rotational or continuous-grazing pastures where persistence under heavy animal pressure matters more than peak hay yield.
